query: For high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability to develop and retain a protective oxide layer that provides oxidation resistance? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison that would reveal it, the observations expected relative to a baseline, the applicable boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The ability of the high-entropy alloy to develop and retain a protective oxide layer is governed by the selective oxidation of aluminum. At high temperatures under oxidizing (air) conditions, Al diffuses outward much more rapidly than other elements forming a continuous, duplex oxide scale (an external Al2O3 layer over an inner Cr2O3-rich region) that protects the substrate by limiting further oxygen ingress. Under low-oxygen conditions, such as vacuum, the limited outward diffusion of Al produces only a thin alumina film, leading to a less pronounced subsurface phase transformation.
generation.material_initial_state: Arc-melted, polished, nominally equiatomic AlCrCoFeNi high-entropy alloy with a dual-phase BCC (~79%) and ordered B2 (~21%) structure and a maze-like, spinodally decomposed microstructure (EDS showing ~17.26 at.% Al).
generation.intervention: Heating in situ from room temperature to 1100 °C at 10 °C/min in steps (with a 5 min hold at each 50 °C increment) under two conditions: atmospheric air and low-oxygen/vacuum.
generation.conditions: Controlled heating with HTXRD tracking phase and oxide evolution; comparisons made between atmospheric air (ambient oxygen pressure) and vacuum (p(O2) ≈ 8.82×10^-7 atm) over the temperature range up to 1100 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: The high-temperature exposure drives the initial BCC/B2 matrix to transform through intermediate phases (FCC and Cr-Fe-rich sigma) as a consequence of localized Al-depletion caused by its selective oxidation. The formation of the external Al2O3 scale (with a secondary inner Cr2O3 layer) mediates the oxidation resistance.
generation.mechanism: Selective oxidation occurs primarily via the outward diffusion of Al, which reacts with oxygen to form a robust, continuous alumina scale. This scale, and the accompanying formation of a Cr-rich inner layer, effectively slows further oxidation by acting as a barrier. Under low oxygen conditions, the slower diffusion kinetics result in a thinner protective film.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-cast, unheated baseline (BCC/B2 with no thermally grown oxide) and the vacuum-treated alloy, the air-treated alloy will exhibit earlier onset and more extensive oxidation with formation of a thicker duplex oxide scale (external Al2O3 and inner Cr2O3) along with a pronounced subsurface region depleted in Al and showing phase transformations (FCC and transient sigma phases). In contrast, vacuum exposure will produce only a thin predominantly alumina film with minimal substrate transformation.
generation.baseline: The polished as-cast alloy at room temperature consisting mainly of BCC/B2 phases with no thermally grown oxide scale; the vacuum-exposed condition serves as a lower-oxidation reference relative to atmospheric air.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to the studied composition of the arc‐melted AlCrCoFeNi high-entropy alloy when heated up to 1100 °C under controlled oxidation (air) vs low-oxygen (vacuum) conditions. It is constrained to the temperature range where phase changes (onset of FCC and sigma formation) and oxidation become pronounced (approximately 550 °C for FCC, 600–650 °C for sigma, and 900–1000 °C for oxidation).
generation.uncertainty: There is some uncertainty in the exact temperature thresholds for the phase transformation and the rate of Al depletion, as well as potential minor contributions from other diffusing species (e.g., Cr) under varying oxygen partial pressures. The precise morphology of the oxide layers and the kinetics of scale formation may vary with slight changes in processing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct in situ HTXRD experiments during controlled heating from room temperature to 1100 °C under both atmospheric air and vacuum conditions. Follow up with SEM-BSE cross-sectional imaging and EDX mapping to assess oxide scale morphology, thickness, and elemental partitioning (especially Al depletion) in the subsurface region. Compare these observations with Thermo-Calc/CALPHAD equilibrium predictions.
measurements: Onset temperatures and evolution of phases (BCC, B2, FCC, sigma) via HTXRD
Oxide scale thickness and duplex structure (Al2O3 and Cr2O3 layers) measured via SEM-BSE cross-sectional imaging
Elemental composition profiles (with emphasis on Al-depletion) across the oxide and substrate using EDX mapping
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experiments do not show a significantly thicker and more duplex oxide scale with pronounced Al depletion and accompanying subsurface phase transformation (FCC and transient sigma phases) in air compared to vacuum—and relative to the as-cast alloy—then the hypothesis that selective Al oxidation governs the formation and retention of a protective oxide layer will be falsified.
